title: Hemiarthroplasty of the hip
subtitle: Cemented hemiarthroplasty for a displaced intracapsular neck of femur fracture

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Hip fracture: management (CG124)

sources.org: Association of Anaesthetists (Griffiths R et al). Anaesthesia 76:225
sources.title: Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020

sources.org: Griffiths R, White SM, Moppett IK et al. Anaesthesia 70:623 (AAGBI, BOA, BGS)
sources.title: Safety guideline: reducing the risk from cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture 2015

indications: Displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck in a patient who does not meet the criteria for total hip replacement (NICE CG124).
Undisplaced intracapsular fracture in selected frail patients according to local practice, where fixation is judged likely to fail.
Surgery on the day of or the day after admission, with medical problems corrected in parallel (NICE CG124).
contraindications: Patients who walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick, are cognitively intact and are medically fit: offer total hip replacement instead (NICE CG124).
Pre-existing symptomatic arthritis of the hip: total hip replacement is usually better.
Pathological fracture from metastasis: needs whole-femur imaging and a construct that protects the whole bone.
Acute medical instability that can be corrected within hours: correct first, then operate.
preparation: Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip radiographs; template head size and stem against the uninjured side.
Orthogeriatric involvement, delirium screening, fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block for analgesia, and correction of anaemia, fluids and electrolytes.
Identify patients at high risk of bone cement implantation syndrome (significant cardiorespiratory disease, pulmonary hypertension, frailty) and plan the cementing with the anaesthetist.

Consent risks to discuss: infection, dislocation, periprosthetic fracture, bleeding and transfusion, venous thromboembolism, leg length difference, nerve injury, bone cement implantation syndrome, delirium, failure to regain previous mobility, and a high risk of death in the months after a hip fracture. Use a mental capacity assessment and a best-interests process where needed.
positioning: Lateral decubitus with pelvic supports, operated side up, with careful padding of frail skin and the down-side heel and fibular head.
Keep the patient warm; hypothermia worsens bleeding and delirium.
equipment: Cemented hemiarthroplasty system with a proven modern stem design, unipolar or bipolar head per local practice; NICE CG124 recommends against Austin Moore or Thompson stems.
Head sizing gauges, broaches, trial heads, cement gun and restrictor, pulsatile lavage.
Cerclage wires or cables for a calcar crack.
anatomy: The femoral head blood supply is mainly from the medial femoral circumflex artery through retinacular vessels along the neck; a displaced intracapsular fracture disrupts it, which is why the head is replaced rather than fixed.
The sciatic nerve lies behind the short external rotators in the posterior approach.
In the anterolateral approach, the superior gluteal nerve runs between gluteus medius and minimus a limited distance above the tip of the trochanter, so the gluteus medius split is kept short.
criticalSafety: Run the cement safety pause: brief the team, ensure the anaesthetist is ready, and use modern cementing technique with a canal plug, lavage, drying and a cement gun.

Approach: NICE CG124 suggests considering an anterolateral approach in preference to a posterior approach. The steps below use the posterior approach shared with total hip replacement; units using the anterolateral approach substitute it and repair the abductors meticulously.
Handle the fragile femur gently during dislocation and broaching.
structuresAtRisk: Femoral shaft and calcar in osteoporotic bone
Skin over pressure areas in a frail patient
commonErrors: Not preparing the team for cementing in a high-risk patient.
Leaving a long neck that makes reduction tight and lengthens the leg.
Weight-bearing restrictions that are not needed and delay mobilisation.
complications: Bone cement implantation syndrome, including intra-operative cardiac arrest.
Dislocation, periprosthetic fracture and leg length difference.
Surgical site infection, haematoma, venous thromboembolism.
Delirium, pressure injury, pneumonia and acute kidney injury.
Acetabular erosion and pain in more active patients, which can need conversion to total hip replacement.
High peri-operative and one-year mortality in frail patients.
postop: Full weight bearing without restriction, and mobilisation the day after surgery (NICE CG124).
Orthogeriatric review, delirium screening, regular paracetamol and opioid as needed, avoiding NSAIDs where renal function or bleeding risk makes them unsafe.
Haemoglobin, renal function and fluid balance checks; thromboprophylaxis per NICE NG89.
Bone health assessment, falls prevention and discharge planning from admission.

steps.emphasis: Assess capacity. If the patient lacks capacity, use the best-interests process and involve the family. Mark the side.
State at the time-out whether the patient is at high risk from cement, and the plan if blood pressure falls.
Frail skin: pad every pressure point, and keep the patient warm.
If your unit uses the anterolateral approach (which NICE CG124 suggests considering), substitute it here.
The head is free in a displaced fracture: remove it with a corkscrew, clear fragments of neck and ligamentum teres, then trim the neck to the templated level.
Osteoporotic bone fractures easily. Broach with control, not force.
Check stability through a functional range, and that the trial neck length does not make the leg longer than the other side.
Follow the cemented hemiarthroplasty safety guideline: canal plug, lavage, drying, retrograde gun delivery, and avoid excessive pressurisation in high-risk patients.
Send the femoral head for histology if there is any suspicion of a pathological fracture.
Record full weight bearing and any reason for restriction, so the physiotherapist can start the next day.

step.hemi.head-sizing.title: Measuring the femoral head and choosing the prosthetic head
step.hemi.head-sizing.why: In a hemiarthroplasty the prosthetic head articulates against native cartilage. A head that is too large sits tight and causes pain; one that is too small concentrates load and can dislocate or erode the acetabulum.
how: Measure the extracted head diameter with the sizing gauge in two planes.
Inspect the acetabular cartilage: significant arthritis changes the decision towards total hip replacement if the patient meets the criteria and it was consented for.
Trial the matching head in the acetabulum: it should sit with a suction fit and rotate freely.
If between sizes, choose by the trial fit rather than rounding up.
structuresAtRisk: Ligamentum teres remnant and fat pad (interposition)
pitfalls: Leaving ligamentum teres or labral fragments in the acetabulum, which block seating.
